next.name: Storm-1567
next.headline: Storm-1567 (Akira): ransomware crew that reports say hits VMware ESXi servers
next.in_short: Storm-1567 is also called Akira, PUNK SPIDER and GOLD SAHARA. Reports describe a busy ransomware operation that goes after VMware ESXi servers. Counts of its victims come from a few sources, some unnamed.

sentences.t: Storm-1567 is also known as Akira, PUNK SPIDER and GOLD SAHARA.
Mandiant lists REDBIKE (Akira) among the prolific groups in its M-Trends 2026 report, which draws on 2025 incident investigations.
Rapid7 says the 2025 threat landscape was dominated by Akira, Cl0p and Warlock.
Halcyon says the group Scattered Spider has been linked to several ransomware payloads, Akira among them.
Red Canary says the activity it tracks as Storm-0844 was historically tied to Akira ransomware. It says that activity has recently switched to deploying FOG ransomware.
SecurityScorecard says Akira has emerged as a significant threat in recent years, particularly targeting VMware ESXi servers.
Sygnia names Akira among the ransomware groups and tools that attack VMware ESXi virtualization environments.

Sygnia says ransomware attacks on ESXi typically follow a similar pattern. Its steps are initial access, privilege escalation, access validation, backup compromise, data theft, shutdown of virtual machines and encryption.
Sygnia says attackers often try double extortion. They steal data first, then encrypt systems.
Sygnia also says attackers sometimes encrypt or delete logs to hide their activity.
CYFIRMA reports that ransomware groups in general infiltrate VMware ESXi using SSH tunnels. The report does not tie this to Akira alone.
CYFIRMA reports that Akira was a significant threat in January 2025, with 72 victims. It says the group's activity rose 60% that month.
SecurityScorecard says Akira has been responsible for nine major breaches. It bases this on 'recent threat attribution data' and does not name the source.
Treat virtualization hosts as high-value targets. Keep backups separate from the systems they protect, and watch administrator access to hypervisors closely.
